Prop 40, BSZ side: the reproduction

Boll, Saez and Zucman (BSZ, 2026) and the Galle, Gamage, Saez and Shanske (GGSS) expert report, reproduced step by step from the authors’ August 2026 workbook

Published

October 7, 2026

BSZ side of California Proposition 40: Open Output (the explorer) · Open Analysis: Report (here) and Slides · Open Materials · Overview

Introduction

California’s Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act, would levy a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of California’s billionaires, paid 1% a year over five years. Two documents carry the BSZ side’s revenue estimate, and this report reproduces both:

  1. Boll, Saez and Zucman (BSZ), California Billionaires: Wealth, Taxes, and Wealth Tax Revenue Estimates, NBER Working Paper 35218, August 2026 revision, and its supplementary Excel workbook. Table 5, row 1 estimates the tax at $103.8 billion.
  2. Galle, Gamage, Saez and Shanske (GGSS), Expert Report on Proposition 40, updated 20 July 2026. It cites $100 billion, and says on p.4 where that comes from: “Factoring in 10% of tax avoidance and evasion leads to a scoring of $104 billion that we round to $100 billion for simplicity.” So the GGSS number is the BSZ row-1 computation, rounded. Reproducing one reproduces the other.

This report is part of an Open Policy Analysis of the BSZ side:

  • Open Output: the explorer, where the assumptions move and the revenue follows
  • Open Analysis: this document, and the slide deck
  • Open Materials: the materials page, every script, test and data file

The preferred estimate is Table 5, row 1: $103.8 billion of one-time wealth tax revenue, with $3.7 billion of extra state income tax from asset sales and an income tax loss of $0.15 billion a year. It is the benchmark both documents lead with, and the one the campaign cites. Rows 2 to 4 of Table 5 are the authors’ own sensitivity checks; this report reproduces them and the explorer shows them next to the preferred row, but none of them replaces it. That follows the project’s pre-specified output (PLAN.md, “Pre-specified output”), fixed before any result was seen: the strongest version of each side, its two documents side by side.

What “reproduced” means here. The pipeline re-derives every formula cell of the authors’ workbook in R and checks each against the workbook’s own cached value. It does not re-collect the raw data: the Forbes wealth figures, the tax statistics and the SEC filings enter as the workbook records them. So the reproduction shows that the arithmetic from those inputs to the published tables is what the paper says it is. It does not show that the inputs are right.

How to read this report

Text in blockquotes is quoted from the paper. Everything else is ours. Page numbers are PDF pages of the August 2026 working paper; the printed folio runs two lower in the main text. Every number in running text is computed when this page is rendered, from the pipeline’s stored results (open any “code” fold to see which one). Tables and figures are the pipeline’s own gt and ggplot2 objects. The figures keep the May 2026 numbering the pipeline was first built against; where August renumbered, the text says so.

Notation, in one place

Symbol Meaning Value in row 1
\(\tau\) wealth tax rate (one time) 5%
\(W_0\) wealth of California billionaires on 1 July 2026 $2,307 billion
\(n_0\) number of those billionaires 250
\(\alpha\) share of wealth lost to avoidance and evasion 10%
\(m\) share of that avoidance that is people leaving the state 50%
\(s\) share of the tax paid by selling assets 1/3
\(g\) share of a sale’s price that is a taxable gain 80%
\(t_{cg}\) top California tax rate on gains 13.3%
\(C\) California income tax billionaires pay per year, 2019-2025 average $3.06 billion

Two letters are reused locally, following the paper: in Section II, \(g_t\) is the yearly growth of billionaire wealth (not the gain share \(g\) above), and in the Laffer-curve section \(e\) is a semi-elasticity, while the \(e\) raised to a power there is the exponential.

II. The wealth of California billionaires

A. Short-run growth: Table 1 Panel A and Figure 1

Table 1 Panel A provides basic statistics on California billionaires in recent years. (BSZ PDF p.5)

What is computed. For each year, total billionaire wealth is the sum of the Forbes wealth of every California resident on the list, \[W_t = \sum_{i \in \text{CA}_t} w_{i,t},\] with Larry Ellison excluded throughout, because he left California before 2026. Growth is \(g_t = W_t / W_{t-1} - 1\), and the “2023-2025” row is the cumulative \(W_{2025}/W_{2022} - 1\). In plain words: add up the list, then compare years. The top-4 column adds Page, Brin, Zuckerberg and Huang from the workbook’s SEC-based panel. August added a “1 July 2026” row, and replaced the paper’s old denominator (California GDP) with California’s total adjusted gross income (AGI), the income reported on tax returns.

The 2025 count is 240 billionaires holding $2,055 billion, which is the paper’s own figure (“240 billionaires with total wealth of $2055 billion”, Appendix A). Getting there needed one correction to the workbook, described under What reproduces: four rows of the raw list were pasted twice.

B. The long run: Table 1 Panel B and Figure 2

Figure 2 depicts the longer time series. Panel A depicts the trajectory of top .001% wealth. (BSZ PDF p.8)

What is computed. Over forty years the number of billionaires grows with the population, so the paper follows a fixed share of families instead: in August, the top .001% (May used the top .0002%). Wealth is in real 2026 dollars. The comparison is with average income per family. The “annualized growth” row is the constant yearly rate that turns the 1982 value into the 2026 value: \[\bar g = \left(\frac{X_{2026}}{X_{1982}}\right)^{1/44} - 1.\]

III. Taxes paid by California billionaires

A. California income tax: Table 2, Figure 3 and Table 3

For all California billionaires, we estimate the California income tax they pay using Franchise Tax Board (the California tax administration) tabulated statistics, a Pareto extrapolation, and an adjustment based on Federal tax data. (BSZ PDF p.10)

Why an extrapolation. Tax statistics are published by income bracket, not by name, and the top bracket holds thousands of filers, not the 240 billionaires. The paper assumes the top of the income distribution follows a Pareto law: above any cutoff \(t\), average income is a constant multiple \(b\) of \(t\). From the top bracket’s filer count \(n_t\) and total income \(A_t\), \[b = \frac{A_t / n_t}{t}, \qquad \hat t_N = t \left(\frac{n_t}{N}\right)^{1 - 1/b},\] where \(\hat t_N\) is the cutoff above which exactly \(N\) filers sit (\(N\) = the number of billionaires). Their average income is \(b\,\hat t_N\), and applying the bracket’s average tax rate gives the tax the top \(N\) earners pay.

From top earners to top wealth holders. Billionaires are not the top earners: the paper cites Balkir et al. (2025) and the Survey of Consumer Finances for top wealth holders’ income being about half of top earners’ income (\(\theta = 0.5\)), plus a small correction for the extrapolation overshooting on US data where the answer is known. The result is the “all California billionaires” column of Table 2. Its 2019-2025 average, $3.06 billion a year, is the \(C\) that Table 5 uses below.

The top-4 columns need no extrapolation: the workbook computes each person’s income tax from their SEC filings (stock sales, dividends, option exercises).

B. All taxes paid by billionaires: Figure 4

What is computed. Figure 4 adds federal income tax, corporate tax and property and sales tax to the state income tax, each as a share of wealth. Corporate tax is attributed to billionaires in proportion to what they own. For private businesses, which file no public accounts, the workbook scales the public-company tax rate by the split of private wealth between pass-through and private C-corporations. August changed two of those weights and the gross-up for diversified holdings (11% in May, 9.5% in August); see RC2 below.

Figure 4: tar_read(fig4) 
tr("fig4")

C. All taxes paid by the top 4: Table 4 and Figures 5 to 7

Table 4 provides detailed numbers of wealth, income earned, and taxes paid by type of tax for the top 4 over the full 2019-2025 period. (BSZ PDF p.15)

What is computed. For the four largest fortunes the workbook builds taxes bottom up from company filings: each person’s share \(s_{i,t}\) of company profits and corporate taxes, \[\Pi_{i,t} = s_{i,t}\,\Pi_{\text{firm},t},\] plus imputed property tax (1% of property, plant and equipment) and sales tax. “Economic income” adds retained company profits to the income that shows up on a tax return, because a founder’s share of profits the company keeps is income to them even though it is never taxed as such. Figure 5 compares taxes with fiscal income, economic income and wealth gains; Figure 6 runs the tax rates back to 2004; Figure 7 compares them with economy-wide averages.

IV. The economics of taxing billionaires’ wealth

A. The one-time 5% tax: Table 5, step by step

This is the section the BSZ side’s headline rests on. Table 5 has four rows. Row 1 is the benchmark; rows 2 to 4 change one assumption at a time. We build row 1 in five steps, then each other row as a change to it.

Step 1: the tax base

Using the July 1st wealth value of $2.3 trillion, the wealth tax scores at $104 billion (=90%*5%*$2307 billion). (BSZ PDF p.24)

The base is Forbes’ real-time list on 1 July 2026: \(n_0\) = 250 billionaires with \(W_0\) = $2,307 billion. These two numbers are typed into the workbook (Tab5!B6:C6); they are data, but data the authors read off Forbes on that day, not something the pipeline recomputes. The Act itself values wealth on 31 December 2026, so the real base will differ; GGSS note that the daily estimate ranged from $87 billion to $107 billion between January and mid-July 2026 (GGSS p.4, fn.8).

Step 2: avoidance and evasion

Some wealth will escape the tax, through under-valuation, hiding, or leaving the state in time. The authors assume a share \(\alpha\) = 10% of all of these together: \[W^{\text{tax}} = (1 - \alpha)\,W_0 = 0.9 \times 2,307 = 2,076.3.\] In words: the tax is charged on 90% of listed wealth. The 10% is not estimated. GGSS argue it is small because most of the wealth is listed stock that is easy to value, and each of some 250 taxpayers can be audited individually (GGSS p.4). It is guesswork, and the single most important one for the headline: it is the only guess the revenue number itself depends on (see Every input, by origin).

Step 3: wealth tax revenue

\[T = \tau\,W^{\text{tax}} = 0.05 \times 2,076.3 = 103.8.\] That is the preferred estimate: $103.8 billion, collected once (in five annual installments). Before avoidance, 5% of the base would be $115.4 billion; avoidance costs $11.5 billion.

Step 4: extra state income tax from selling assets

Table 5 reports a column of this extra CA income tax generated assuming that wealth taxes will be paid one-third by selling assets triggering taxable realized capital gains (with a basis of 20% of selling price …) and two-thirds with liquidities or debt. (BSZ PDF p.24)

To pay the tax, some billionaires sell shares, and selling realises capital gains that the state taxes. With a share \(s\) of the tax paid by selling, a share \(g\) of each sale being gain, and the top state rate \(t_{cg}\) on gains: \[E = s \cdot g \cdot t_{cg} \cdot T = \tfrac13 \times 0.80 \times 0.133 \times 103.8 = 3.68.\] So the tax pays back about 3.5% of itself in income tax, spread over the five payment years. The one-third is guesswork; the 80% gain share is the paper’s own estimate of how much of billionaire wealth is unrealised gains.

Step 5: income tax lost to billionaires who leave

If we assume that half of the 10% avoidance takes the form of mobility: i.e. 5% of billionaires were able to successfully relocate outside California in the narrow time window before January 1st, 2026, then we estimate that a corresponding 5% of the total California individual income tax paid by billionaires will be lost. (BSZ PDF p.24)

A billionaire who leaves stops paying California income tax. The authors assume half of the avoidance (\(m\) = 50%) is people leaving, so \(\alpha m\) = 5% of the income tax billionaires pay is lost: \[L = -\alpha\,m\,C = -0.10 \times 0.5 \times 3.06 = -0.153 \text{ per year}.\] This is a yearly loss, and Table 5 does not say for how many years. The paper argues that, for a genuinely one-time tax, departures should be temporary, “say only 5 years” (PDF p.27). The RJKDC report (Rauh, Jaros, Kearney, Doran and Cosso) counts the loss forever. That difference in horizon is the largest single dispute between the two sides (comparison/DISPUTES.md, row 2) and is outside this side’s output.

Row 2: adding the billionaires Forbes misses

If we assume that the tail is Pareto with constant b=4.48 between $1 billion and $4.5 billion, then this means that there should be around 617 California billionaires (instead of the 249 listed by Forbes). (BSZ PDF p.25)

Above $4.5 billion, average wealth over any threshold is a steady multiple of the threshold, \(b\) = 4.48: the signature of a Pareto distribution. Below $4.5 billion the Forbes list’s \(b\) climbs towards 9, which is what a list missing many small fortunes looks like. Holding \(b\) at 4.48 down to $1 billion adds 368 billionaires and $615 billion to the 15 April 2026 list the workbook used, that is 148% more people but only 28.2% more wealth. Row 2 applies those two percentages to the 1 July base, with a higher avoidance rate \(\alpha_s\) = 20% for these less visible fortunes, and subtracts a deduction for those in the $1 to $1.1 billion band, where the Act phases the rate in: \[T_2 = \tau\left[(1-\alpha)W_0 + (1-\alpha_s)\,\Delta W\right] - 0.025\,f_{ph}\,\Delta W, \qquad \Delta W = 28.2\% \times W_0,\] with \(f_{ph}\) = 12.1% the share of the added wealth in the phase-in band. The result is $127.9 billion.

Row 3: an aggressive assumption on who has left

The third row in Table 5 scores the wealth tax assuming that Page, Thiel, Hankey, Kalanick successfully moved before January 1, 2026 which is an aggressive assumption. (BSZ PDF p.26)

Two groups are treated differently. Four people are assumed to have left before 1 January 2026, so they escape the tax altogether and stop paying income tax. Three more (Brin, Zuckerberg, Fang) pay the tax but are assumed to leave later, so only their income tax is lost. For the top three, lost income tax on company wealth is their SEC-based average from Table 3; on everything else it is proportional to wealth, at the rate billionaires pay outside the top four’s company wealth, 0.201% of wealth a year (Tab5!F18/B18):

the seven named leavers: tar_read(site_scoring_inputs)$leavers 
lv <- inp$leavers
lv$name <- tools::toTitleCase(lv$name)
lv$wealth <- bn(lv$wealth)
lv$annual_inctax_loss <- bn(lv$annual_inctax_loss, 3)
names(lv) <- c("Person", "Assumed timing", "Wealth, $B", "Income tax lost, $B/yr")
show(lv)
Person Assumed timing Wealth, $B Income tax lost, $B/yr
Page pre-2026 (escapes the wealth tax) 294.6 0.103
Thiel pre-2026 (escapes the wealth tax) 27.3 0.055
Hankey pre-2026 (escapes the wealth tax) 8.2 0.016
Kalanick pre-2026 (escapes the wealth tax) 3.6 0.007
Brin post-2026 (pays it, then leaves) 271.7 0.078
Zuckerberg post-2026 (pays it, then leaves) 210.3 0.100
Fang post-2026 (pays it, then leaves) 1.5 0.003

Taxable wealth falls to \(0.9\,(W_0 - W_{pre})\) with \(W_{pre}\) = $333.6 billion, and revenue to $88.8 billion. The yearly income tax loss grows to $0.52 billion, still small, because the SEC data show the top three pay little income tax relative to their wealth. Whether any of these people has actually changed legal residence is a legal judgment, and the most important guesswork in the whole dispute (comparison/DISPUTES.md, row 3).

Row 4: rows 2 and 3 together

Row 4 adds the Pareto billionaires to row 3: $114.8 billion, with a yearly income tax loss of $0.56 billion. One detail: row 4 does not subtract the phase-in deduction that row 2 subtracts for the same added billionaires (Tab5!F9 against Tab5!F7). We reproduce the workbook as it is; a consistent treatment would lower row 4 by $2.0 billion. We list this under What reproduces.

every Table 5 cell against the workbook’s cached value 
xl <- read_sheet("Tab5", range = "B6:H9")
cols <- c("n_billionaires", "wealth", "taxable_wealth", "avoidance_rate",
          "wealth_tax_revenue", "extra_ca_inctax_sales", "annual_ca_inctax_loss")
dev <- abs(as.matrix(t5[, cols]) - as.matrix(xl))
t5_cells <- length(dev); t5_maxdev <- max(dev)

All 28 cells match the workbook’s cached values; the largest absolute difference is 1.4e-16.

every Table 5 cell against the digit printed in the paper: tar_read(site_tab5_printed) 
pr <- tr("site_tab5_printed")
miss <- pr[!pr$matches_printed, ]
miss_txt <- paste0("row ", miss$row, " (printed ", formatC(miss$printed, format = "f", digits = 2),
                   ", workbook ", formatC(miss$reproduced, format = "f", digits = 3), ")")

Matching the printed table is a stricter test, because the paper rounds. Of the 28 printed cells, 26 are what the reproduced value rounds to. The other 2 are both in the income tax loss column: row 2 (printed -0.19, workbook -0.196) and row 3 (printed -0.51, workbook -0.515). The workbook’s own cached values agree with ours, and the paper’s text quotes the printed figures ($0.19 billion on PDF p.25, $0.51 billion on p.26), so the paper rounds these two cells differently from its own workbook. Both are a cent of a billion; neither changes an argument.

How far the guesses move the result

The explorer holds every combination of the six assumptions. Here each one moves on its own, with the others at row 1:

one-at-a-time ranges from tar_read(site_grid) 
dials <- site_dials()
keys  <- vapply(dials, `[[`, "", "key")
base  <- stats::setNames(mapply(function(d, j) d$levels[j], dials, site_named_rows()[[1]]), keys)
lvl   <- function(d, v) switch(d$fmt, pct = paste0(round(100 * v), "%"),
                               bool = if (v == 1) "yes" else "no",
                               frac3 = c("none", "1/3", "2/3", "all")[round(3 * v) + 1])
alone <- function(key) {   # grid cells where only `key` differs from row 1
  Reduce(`&`, lapply(setdiff(keys, key), function(k) abs(grid[[k]] - base[[k]]) < 1e-9))
}
rng <- do.call(rbind, lapply(dials, function(d) {
  g <- grid[alone(d$key), ]
  data.frame(
    input = d$label, origin = d$origin,
    tried = paste(lvl(d, min(d$levels)), "to", lvl(d, max(d$levels))),
    `revenue, $B` = paste(bn(min(g$wealth_tax_revenue)), "to", bn(max(g$wealth_tax_revenue))),
    `income tax lost, $B/yr` = paste(bn(-max(g$annual_ca_inctax_loss), 2), "to",
                                     bn(-min(g$annual_ca_inctax_loss), 2)),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))

GGSS start from the same 250 people and $2,307 billion, take 5% ($115 billion), apply the same 10% avoidance and get $104 billion, which they round to $100 billion. The expert report’s other figures also come from BSZ Table 5: the $128 billion with missing billionaires (row 2, reproduced as $127.9 billion) and “about $20 billion/year” (one fifth of the rounded total, the annual installment).

B. A permanent annual wealth tax: the Laffer curve

This part estimates a different policy, a wealth tax charged every year, which is not what Proposition 40 proposes. The paper uses it to answer the argument that billionaires will leave for fear of future taxes. The pipeline’s “Figure 8” is the August paper’s Figure 9 (August inserted a new Figure 8 on venture capital, which the pipeline does not build).

With a semi-elasticity e, the wealth tax rate that maximizes tax revenue while taking into account mobility responses is τ=1/e. (BSZ PDF p.28)

What is computed. A semi-elasticity \(e\) says each extra percentage point of tax shrinks the base by about \(e\) percent through people moving away. With a base of \(Z_0\) = $2,000 billion at today’s tax (the workbook’s rounded input) and \(\tau_0\) = 0.2% of wealth, the income tax billionaires already pay, \[Z(\tau) = Z_0\, e^{-e(\tau - \tau_0)}, \qquad T(\tau) = \tau\, Z(\tau).\] Revenue peaks where the next point of tax loses as much base as it gains in rate, at \(\tau = 1/e\). With \(e\) = 10 (Brülhart et al. 2022, the same value Rauh et al. use) that is 10%. The long-run curve also erodes wealth itself: \(d\) = 15 years of paying the tax shrinks fortunes by \((1-\tau)^d\), and revenue then peaks at 3.9%, close to the paper’s \(1/(1+d+e) = 3.8\%\).

Every input, by origin

This section is not in the paper. It sorts every input of the one-time estimate by how much evidence stands behind it, which is the first question a reader who wants to argue with the result has to answer.

  • data: read off a public source, and in principle re-collectable from it.
  • research: an estimate from a published study, including the authors’ own.
  • guesswork: set by assumption; argued for, but not measured.
  • scenario: a choice about which policy is being estimated.
  • derived: implied by other rows. convention: a date.

how many of each kind 
# Which guesses move the headline revenue? Vary each dial alone around row 1.
moves_rev <- vapply(dials, function(d) diff(range(grid$wealth_tax_revenue[alone(d$key)])) > 1e-9, TRUE)
is_guess  <- vapply(dials, `[[`, "", "origin") == "guesswork"
guess_moving_rev <- vapply(dials[moves_rev & is_guess], `[[`, "", "label")
n_guess_dials <- sum(is_guess)
stopifnot(sum(ins$origin == "guesswork") == n_guess_dials)

The headline. Of the 18 inputs, 5 are guesswork, and they are exactly the explorer’s 5 guesswork dials. Only 2 of them move the revenue number when varied on their own (avoidance and evasion; aggressive assumption on leavers); the others move only the smaller income tax columns, or matter only in the scenario rows. So the preferred $103.8 billion is Forbes’ list, times 5%, times one minus a single guessed avoidance rate; the only other guess that moves it is who has already left. The disputes with the RJKDC report are mostly about inputs this table labels guesswork or scenario: who has left (disputes row 3), how long losses last, and whether a one-time tax triggers permanent departures.

The suite ran on 2026-09-23 against the august workbook: 561 expectations passed and 0 failed. The compute, tables and data_sheets files compare R against the workbook’s own cached cells, formula by formula, at a stated tolerance; snapshots pins every output so any change fails; site pins the explorer to the reproduction. Figures are checked for structure and a few anchor values, not pixel by pixel.

Mismatches found, and how each was resolved

The August workbook was first run through code written for the May version, and 184 expectations failed. Every failure was traced to one of ten root causes before anything was fixed (VERIFY-AUGUST.md):

Cause What it was Resolution
RC1 shortrunseries: August moved most columns and dropped one column map per vintage (R/vintage.R)
RC2 billionairesCAinctax: two rows inserted; the diversified-holdings gross-up changed from 11% to 9.5% and two private-wealth weights changed row map per vintage; new parameters ported
RC3 Table 5’s typed-in base and leaver wealth moved to the 1 July 2026 Forbes values constants per vintage
RC4 Table 1 and A1 denominators changed from GDP to AGI ported from the formulas
RC5 a “2026 (July 1st)” row inserted in Tables 1 and A1 ported
RC6 Panel B redefined from the top .0002% to the top .001%, endpoint 2025 to 2026 ported
RC7 Table 2 gained two columns; its average row changed formula ported
RC8 the Laffer sheet moved from Fig8 to Fig9 sheet name per vintage
RC9 four smaller literals (row counts, a sheet count, one cell) updated
RC10 a genuine data error in the workbook, below de-duplicated

A data-entry error in the workbook. In August’s data_sec_all sheet, rows 1338 to 1341 (four 2025 entries: Sijbrandij, Rihanna, Preston-Werner, Stephens) appear a second time at rows 1342 to 1345. Counting both copies gives 244 billionaires; dropping the repeat gives 240, which matches the workbook’s own aggregate sheet and the paper’s text. The pipeline drops rows that repeat year, person and wealth exactly (R/compute_data_sec_agg.R).

Two printed cells that differ from the workbook. Table 5’s income tax loss in rows 2 and 3 is printed as $0.19 and $0.51 billion; the workbook, and this reproduction, give values that round to $0.20 and $0.52 (see Table 5, reproduced).

Readings the workbook leaves implicit. Both are kept at the workbook’s behaviour and disclosed on the explorer:

  • Tab5!H6 types the income tax loss share as a literal 0.05. We read it as avoidance times the leaving share (0.10 × 0.5), as the row label says. It matters only when the explorer moves those inputs.
  • Row 4 omits row 2’s phase-in deduction (Tab5!F9), worth $2.0 billion.

Display labels that lag the data. Tables 1 and A1 hold August values under some May labels (GDP for AGI, 2025 for 2026, .0002% for .001%, 2025 dollars for 2026 dollars), and a few summary cells render as rounded zeros. The numbers are tested; the labels are not. Fixing them changes the pinned table snapshots, so it is left for a separate change.

What is not reproduced.

  • August’s new Figure 8 (venture capital deals) and new Appendix Figure A1 (wealth relative to AGI) have no builder yet.
  • The raw inputs are not re-collected (Forbes, Franchise Tax Board, SEC, IRS, national accounts), except a one-person SEC proof of concept. An error in the workbook’s inputs would pass straight through.
  • The GGSS July report has no workbook of its own. Its $100 billion is reproduced only in the sense above: it is BSZ row 1, rounded.

Reproducing this document

cd bsz-analysis
Rscript -e 'targets::tar_make(names = !tidyselect::any_of(c("report_html","report_pdf")))'
Rscript tools/site-test-results.R      # writes site/data/test-results.csv
cd site && quarto render repro.qmd

The workbook is not redistributed; DATA-SOURCES.csv gives its URL and SHA-256. Set CAWTBSZ_MATERIALS if it lives outside bsz-analysis/original-materials/.
